title: It begins!
summary: The goal this week is simple: baby starts to learn what happens at the table. Milk or formula stays the main source of nutrition, so don't dwell on how much actually gets swallowed. Baby is practising the motions: bringing food to the mouth, biting, moving food around with the tongue, mashing with the gums.

Every food comes two ways: a finger food to hold and munch, and a mash on a pre-loaded spoon. Only finger foods or only purées is fine too. Eat alongside baby and show how it's done; baby learns by watching you.
Don't force it. If baby cries, purses the lips or refuses, stop. A fussy or sick day is a good day to skip solids and try again tomorrow.
tip: If baby isn't reaching for food on the tray, hold it in the air in front of them and let go once they grab it. Same with a pre-loaded spoon.

title: First allergens: egg and peanut
summary: Early introduction of common food allergens may prevent allergies later in life, so this week gets straight into egg and peanut, two of the most common allergens in babies.
Each allergen is paired with foods from Week 1 that baby already knows. That way, if there is a reaction, you can pinpoint the cause.

Start small and follow the quantity in each day's How to Serve. If there is no sign of a reaction after the first bite, offer more. Serve the allergen early in the day so you can watch for a delayed reaction while baby is awake and a doctor is reachable.
tip: Severe eczema or an existing food allergy? Talk to a paediatric allergist before introducing allergens; both raise the risk of food allergy.

title: Keep the allergens coming
summary: Egg again?! Once an allergen is safely ruled out, repeat it at least twice a week. Regular exposure is what helps baby's body build tolerance; introducing it once and stopping gives no benefit.
Foods keep coming two ways. Let baby hold the spoon, even the wrong way round. For a baby used to being spoon-fed, hold the pre-loaded spoon in front of them and take a bite yourself to model it.
First family meal idea: antipasto salad. Pull vegetables from your own portion to share. Even one shared family meal a week is protective against picky eating.
Keep iron in mind from here on. Baby's iron stores run low between 4 and 6 months, and milk or formula gives very little. Swap in or add an iron-rich food on any day.

title: Letting baby self-feed purées
summary: Letting baby control how they eat, even with purées, helps prevent picky eating later. This week has plenty of naturally puréed foods: bean dip, oatmeal, polenta, yogurt.

To self-feed a purée, scoop some in front of baby and let them see, smell, touch and taste it. With a spoon, pre-load it and place it in front of baby or pass it in the air for them to grab. Baby being in charge of the utensil is key.

A meal where baby takes only a few bites, or none, is still normal and does not mean they won't grow to like the food. Follow baby's cues. Consider doubling the recipes and sharing this week's meals with baby.

title: Bread and wheat
summary: This week introduces bread, made of wheat on purpose: wheat is one of the most common food allergens in children, and early introduction may help prevent allergy.

Which bread? A crusty country loaf is a great finger food because it holds its shape and is less likely to go gummy and stick to the roof of the mouth than soft sliced bread. Dull sharp crust ends with a knife. Toasted iron-fortified sliced bread is another good choice.

Pick a style with minimal ingredients (wheat, water, yeast). Egg in bread is fine once egg is ruled out. Avoid bread made with honey before the first birthday, and check labels for other allergens like dairy, sesame, soy and tree nuts. A little sodium won't hurt baby.

title: First meat: the chicken drumstick
summary: Meat is one of the best sources of iron, which baby needs a lot of right now. It doesn't have to be puréed: a safely prepared chicken drumstick (see the family meal on Day 36) is one of the best finger foods at this stage. It is easy to grab, can be shared at the table, and its firm texture builds jaw strength and tongue coordination for chewing.
If a chunk breaks off in baby's mouth, stay calm. Babies have innate reflexes to spit out food that isn't safe to swallow. Let baby work it out; don't put your fingers in or startle them.
Prefer a different meat? Adapt the menu. The plan also has directions for beef bolognese, chicken liver pâté, lamb meatballs, pork ribs and more.

title: Soy: edamame and tofu
summary: Soy is packed with iron, omega-3s and protein, and is also a common allergen. The good news: under 1% of children are allergic, and over half outgrow it by age six. Soy is in bread, miso, tamari and many prepared foods, so introducing it early and serving it often pays off.

Choose low-sodium forms. Edamame is bright green, quick and delicious; make a big batch of mashed edamame and freeze it for up to 2 months. Firm and extra-firm tofu have far more protein, iron and zinc than silken tofu.
Serve edamame and tofu alongside vitamin C-rich foods, which help baby absorb much more iron from the legumes. This week's menu pairs them for you; mix and match freely.

title: Coconut and chicken liver
summary: Coconut is full of healthy fats for brain and nervous system development. The plan uses desiccated flakes and unsweetened full-fat canned coconut milk (ideally BPA-free).

Coconut counts as a tree nut allergen in the US, though allergy to it is rare. In the plan authors' view it need not be repeated on a strict schedule once introduced. Not a fan? Swap it for milk, stock or water.

Chicken liver is one of the most nutritious first foods: complete protein, iron, B vitamins, choline, vitamin A. It has so much vitamin A that 1 to 2 tablespoons a week is plenty. Its mineral taste pairs well with sweet fruit, so it comes with blueberry sauce. Skip liver? Mashed beans make up the iron and protein.

title: Two meals a day, and finned fish
summary: The 8-month mark is a good time to offer two solid meals a day. Milk or formula is still the main nutrition and meals may still be mostly play, but twice a day gives baby more chances to learn that mealtime also fills the belly.

If baby seems uninterested, they may simply be full from milk. Try extending the gap between a milk feed and a meal by up to an hour. Skipping a meal or a whole day is fine; pick up tomorrow. Share meals whenever you can so baby can watch you.
Finned fish is a common allergen, and salmon is among the most common fish allergens. The menu uses salmon because it is widely available; any other low-mercury fish works as a substitute.

title: Pincer grasp and bite-sized pieces
summary: Between 8 and 9 months many babies start to bring thumb and pointer finger together: the pincer grasp. That is the signal to start offering bite-sized pieces, about the size of your thumb knuckle. Small enough to pick up and fit in the mouth, not so small it can block an airway (which is about the width of a chickpea right now).

Foods now often come as a mash or large piece baby already knows, plus bite-sized pieces to practise the pincer grasp. Offering both sizes keeps frustration low. Nervous about the small size? Stick with mashes and large pieces for now.

Eleven new foods this week, including the first tree nut (almond; choose another if you prefer). Slow down, repeat a menu or skip a meal if the pace feels too much. There are more family meals from here on: eating alongside adults is one of the best ways for baby to learn, and protects against picky eating later.

title: Ten allergens and counting
summary: Cashew makes it ten common allergens introduced, and from here one new tree nut arrives each week. Each introduced allergen should keep appearing at least twice a week to build tolerance.

Juggling 10+ allergens a week is easier with a few shortcuts: keep a batch of mixed nut and seed butter (smooth, honey-free, only nuts already ruled out); skip ahead to Day 90's ground-up granola and add nuts as they are cleared; stock the freezer with meatballs and pancakes made with nut flours and other cleared allergens.
Keep watching for the pincer grasp. When it appears, move down to thumb-knuckle-sized pieces. Not there yet? This week's recipes can still be served mashed or in large pieces.

title: Division of responsibility
summary: About three months in, offer bite-sized pieces if you haven't yet. The pincer grasp (thumb and pointer finger meeting) is the sign baby is ready. Pieces should be thumb-knuckle size; if baby can't manage them yet, practice makes perfect.

Remember the division of responsibility: you decide what, when and how you show up at the meal. Baby decides whether and how much to eat. Never pick up a small piece and push it into baby's mouth; let baby lead.

It is fine to offer mash after baby tires of small pieces, but don't make a purée top-off the routine after every meal, or baby learns to wait for the easy option. If baby needs topping up, offer a bottle or nursing session instead. Milk or formula remains the most critical nutrition until 12 months.

title: Sharing the second meal
summary: No separate family meal this week on purpose: the second meal each day is designed to be shared with baby at whatever mealtime suits you. Three months in, eating alongside adults matters. Don't like a recipe? Swap it for one from your favourite cookbook.

Another tree nut this week (pecan; substitute a different nut if you like). The parade of tree nuts at the end of the plan can feel like a lot, but early introduction builds tolerance and tree nuts also bring iron, which milk and formula lack.
Each introduced allergen still needs to show up at least twice a week. The shortcuts from Week 11 (mixed nut butter, granola, a stocked freezer) make that easier.

title: Almost there
summary: Weeks 14 and 15 wrap up the plan with two solid meals a day, hazelnut as the last tree nut, and plenty of repeat exposure to every allergen introduced so far.

Every baby is unique. Some are still learning to bring food and utensils to the mouth on their own, and that is fine. Others are so good at small pieces that they shovel food in; that is the sign to move back up in size to encourage biting and chewing.
Use the plan to repeat menus and strategies at your own pace. Baby's skills don't need to be perfect. There is a world of food to share, and this is just the beginning.

title: Congratulations!
summary: You are finishing the first 100 days of starting solids. Days 99 and 100 bring together everything so far: a bowl with ground-up granola and every tree nut, a buttery cod bake, and a pizza party to share.

Where to go from here? Keep repeating allergens at least twice a week, keep sharing meals at the table, and keep adjusting piece size to baby's skills: back up in size if baby is shovelling, down to bite-sized when the pincer grasp is solid.
Use this plan to repeat menus and strategies at your own pace. Baby's skills don't need to be perfect; this is just the beginning.
